metadata.preview:
# wcx: count lines, words, bytes and the longest line

Write `wcx.c`, a program that reads standard input to the end and prints exactly one line:

    <lines> <words> <bytes> <maxlen>

four non-negative decimal integers separated by single spaces, followed by a newline.

* `lines`: the number of newline bytes (`\n`) in the input.
* `words`: the number of maximal runs of bytes that are not whitespace. Whitespace is exactly these six bytes:
  space, `\t`, `\n`, `\v`, `\f`, `\r`. Every other byte (including NUL and bytes above 127) belongs to a word.
* `bytes`: the total number of bytes read.
* `maxlen`: the length in bytes of the longest line, not counting its terminating `\n`. A last line without a
  trailing newline counts as a line for this value. A `\r` is an ordinary byte for `maxlen`.

## Constraints

* Plain C11. It must compile cleanly with `gcc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O2 -o wcx wcx.c`.
* **No dynamic memory**: no `malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc`, `getline`, `getdelim` or `strdup`. Memory use must not
  depend on the input: a single line of 64 MiB has to work.

# wcx: count lines, words, bytes and the longest line

Write `wcx.c`, a program that reads standard input to the end and prints exactly one line:

    <lines> <words> <bytes> <maxlen>

four non-negative decimal integers separated by single spaces, followed by a newline.

* `lines`: the number of newline bytes (`\n`) in the input.
* `words`: the number of maximal runs of bytes that are not whitespace. Whitespace is exactly these six bytes:
  space, `\t`, `\n`, `\v`, `\f`, `\r`. Every other byte (including NUL and bytes above 127) belongs to a word.
* `bytes`: the total number of bytes read.
* `maxlen`: the length in bytes of the longest line, not counting its terminating `\n`. A last line without a
  trailing newline counts as a line for this value. A `\r` is an ordinary byte for `maxlen`.

## Constraints

* Plain C11. It must compile cleanly with `gcc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O2 -o wcx wcx.c`.
* **No dynamic memory**: no `malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc`, `getline`, `getdelim` or `strdup`. Memory use must not
  depend on the input: a single line of 64 MiB has to work.
* Exit status 0 on success.

part.text: All tests pass. Let me also test with a file containing longer lines and whitespace edge cases:

All tests pass correctly. Here's the summary:

**Created:** `wcx.c` — a C program that counts lines, words, bytes, and max line-length from stdin.

**Compiled with exact flags from WCX.md:** `gcc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -O2 -o wcx wcx.c` — compiled cleanly, no warnings or errors.

**Verification results:**

| Test | Input | Expected | Got | Pass |
|------|-------|----------|-----|------|
| Empty input | `` | `0 0 0 0` | `0 0 0 0` | ✅ |
| One line | `hello world\n` | `1 2 12 11` | `1 2 12 11` | ✅ |
| Three lines | `abc\ndef\nghi\n` | `3 3 12 3` | `3 3 12 3` | ✅ |
| No trailing newline | `abc\ndef\nghi` | `2 3 11 3` | `2 3 11 3` | ✅ |
| Whitespace lines | `a b\nc d\n` | `2 4 8 3` | `2 4 8 3` | ✅ |
| Longest line mid-file | `ab\ncdefg\nh\n` | `3 3 11 5` | `3 3 11 5` | ✅ |
| Consecutive whitespace/newlines | `a   b\n\n  \tc d\t\n` | `3 4 15 7` | `3 4 15 7` | ✅ |
| NUL/high bytes (`\x00\x7f\xff\n`) | | `1 1 4 3` | `1 1 4 3` | ✅ |

The implementation uses no dynamic memory — only a single character read loop with `fgetc`, so any line length (even 64 MiB) is handled without proportional memory growth.
